- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").

   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

Use the shared [workflow terminology](../../AGENTS.md#workflow-terminology).

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

1. Consolidate findings: merge overlap, resolve contradictions, and note confidence gaps.
2. Define scope: goals, non-goals, delegation items.
3. Write the requirements document using the project’s established conventions in:
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/feature-specification.md`
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/README.md`

   Do not create `SPEC-NNNN-*.md` files — that naming is legacy; `feature-specification.md` is the canonical filename consumed by /geeky-plan and the freeze hooks.

   If a stub README already exists, preserve its stated scope and only update the Status line and missing sections; otherwise create the README stub:

   ```markdown
   # [Feature Name]

   [One-paragraph scope summary.]

   **Status:** Spec written — not yet planned
   **Spec:** `feature-specification.md`
   **Next:** /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/
   ```

Use the 11-section recommended spec structure in `references/spec-structure-template.md` (adapt sections to the feature domain; include citations and explicit assumptions at the end of major findings).

### Phase 5: Commit and Suggest Next Steps

Commit the spec (same command on all platforms). The spec is not yet frozen — it only becomes part of the frozen planning contract after /geeky-plan runs:

```
git add docs/<feature-folder>/
git commit -m "docs: author feature specification in <feature-folder>" -m "[1-line summary of the spec focus]" -m "Research conducted by: codebase analyst, researcher 2 domain, researcher 3 domain"
```

Then suggest next steps:
```
Spec written. Next steps:
- /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/   (to create implementation plan, tasks, kanban)
- /plan-review docs/<feature-folder>/  (to validate the planning package)
- /geeky-implement docs/<feature-folder>/ (to execute)
```

## Research Quality Standards

- **Recency**: Target sources from roughly the past 18 months; avoid older sources unless they cover stable fundamentals.
- **Authority**: Prefer official documentation (Microsoft Learn, AWS docs, RFC specs) over blogs or forums.
- **Specificity**: Include concrete findings (resource types, API versions, package versions, pricing tiers).
- **Adversarial verification**: If researchers disagree on a fact, preserve both positions and flag for user decision.

## Rules

- **Always 3 researchers** — one codebase analyst + two web/domain researchers.
- **Parallel dispatch** — all 3 in a single turn for maximum speed.
- **Research before writing** — do not start the spec document until all researchers report back.
- **Cite sources** — every major claim in the spec should trace to research.
- **Respect existing stubs** — if a README stub exists, treat its stated scope as authoritative unless research justifies adjustments.
- **Follow project conventions** — spec format, naming, and folder structure should match prior specs in `docs/`.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Build `csvledger`, a small Python command-line tool that reads one or more bank-export CSV files of transactions, assigns each transaction a category using a rules file, and prints a monthly report. It must run as `python -m csvledger` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Provide two commands: `report` (per-month, per-category totals) and `categorize` (each transaction with its assigned category). Both commands print either an aligned text table or JSON. Money must be exact (no floating point) and output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. Identical transactions repeated across overlapping exports must be counted once. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
# csvledger: Interface Contract

## Constraints

- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
- **Package location:** `csvledger/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
- **Entry point:** `python -m csvledger <command> ...` run from repo root.

## Functional requirements

- **R1** `python -m csvledger` exposes subcommands `report` and `categorize`; `--help` exits 0.
- **R2** Transaction files are parsed per the CSV contract; any invalid file or row aborts the run with exit 3 and no stdout.
- **R3** The rules file is parsed per the rules contract; any invalid rule aborts with exit 4 and no stdout.
- **R4** Each transaction gets exactly one category: the highest-priority matching rule; ties go to the rule earliest in the file; no match gives `Uncategorized`.
- **R5** Duplicate transactions (same date, stripped description, and numeric amount value) across all inputs are kept once (first occurrence) and a warning is written to stderr. Deduplication runs over all rows of all input files before the `--month` filter; the warning count N covers duplicates across all inputs regardless of `--month`.
- **R6** `report` aggregates by month and category: count, income, expenses, net.
- **R7** `categorize` lists every transaction, sorted by date ascending, ties in input order.
- **R8** `--month YYYY-MM` restricts both commands to transactions in that month.
- **R9** `--format table|json` selects output; default `table`.
- **R10** Money uses `decimal.Decimal`; sums are exact; displayed values are rounded once to 2 dp, ROUND_HALF_UP, never shown as `-0.00`.
- **R11** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, stable ordering, no locale use.

## Interface contract

### Commands

```
python -m csvledger report     [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
python -m csvledger categorize [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
```

- `FILE`: one or more transaction CSV paths, processed in argument order. `-` is an ordinary file name; stdin is never read.
- `--rules`: optional. When omitted, every transaction is `Uncategorized`.
- `--month`: must match `^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$`, else usage error.
- argparse `prog` is `csvledger`. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
- Load order: rules file first, then transaction files in argument order. First error wins.

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success (including empty result and duplicate warnings) |
| 1 | Reserved for unexpected internal error; never intentional |
| 2 | Usage error (argparse: unknown flag, missing FILE, bad `--format`/`--month`) |
| 3 | Transaction file error |
| 4 | Rules file error |

### Transaction CSV

- Encoding UTF-8, optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`); opened with `newline=""`; parsed with `csv.reader` defaults (comma, `"` quoting).
- Line 1 is the header. Header names are stripped and lowercased; `date`, `description`, `amount` are required, in any order; extra columns are ignored; duplicate names are an error.
- Rows with zero fields (blank lines) are skipped. Every other row must have exactly as many fields as the header.
- `date`: stripped value must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a valid calendar date (regex first; do not rely on `date.fromisoformat` alone).
- `amount`: stripped value must match `^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$`. Negative = expense (outflow), positive = income, zero counts but adds to neither.
- `description`: stripped; may be empty.
- A header-only file is valid (zero transactions). A file with no header line (0 bytes) is an error.

### Rules CSV

- Same encoding/header/blank-row/field-count rules. Required columns: `category`, `type`, `pattern`, `priority`.
- `category`: stripped, non-empty. `type`: stripped, exactly `contains` or `regex`. `pattern`: stripped, non-empty. `priority`: stripped, matches `^-?\d+$`.
- `contains`: `pattern.casefold() in description.casefold

n exit with the code shown; stdout stays empty. `<path>` is exactly the argv string given on the command line (a relative path stays relative); `<line>` is `csv.reader.line_num` after reading the record. Row checks run in this order: field count, date, amount (transactions) or field count, category, type, pattern, priority, regex (rules). Header checks run in this order: (1) no header line, (2) duplicate column, (3) missing required column. For a duplicate column, `<name>` is the second occurrence after strip and lowercase, and the first duplicate in header order is reported. For a missing column, `<name>` is the first absent name in the listed order.

| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| File missing/unreadable | 3 / 4 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 / 4 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| No header line | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing header` |
| Duplicate header name (first duplicate in header order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: duplicate column '<name>'` |
| Required column absent (first in listed order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing column '<name>'` |
| Field count mismatch | 3 / 4 | `<path>:<line>: expected <N> fields, got <M>` |
| Bad date | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid date '<value>'` |
| Bad amount | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid amount '<value>'` |

| argparse usage errors | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match the regex `^csvledger( report\| categorize)?: error: ` (argparse subparser prog form allowed) |

Warning (exit unaffected): `csvledger: warning: skipped <N> duplicate row(s)` when N > 0, written after stdout output. `<value>` is the stripped field value.

## Acceptance criteria

Width of each column = max(len(header), longest value) using `len()` on code points. Cells joined by two spaces; each line right-stripped. Line 1: headers. Line 2: dashes of each column width. Then one row per (month, category), sorted by month ascending then category by code-point ascending. No total rows. Zero transactions: header and dash line only.

### `categorize` table

Columns: `DATE` (left), `AMOUNT` (right, per-transaction amount formatted as money), `CATEGORY` (left), `DESCRIPTION` (left). Same width, separator, dash-line and right-strip rules.

### JSON

`json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` followed by `\n`. Money values are strings; counts are integers. Key order is exactly as shown.

- `report`: `{"months": [{"month", "count", "income", "expenses", "net", "categories": [{"category", "count", "income", "expenses", "net"}]}]}`. Months and categories sorted as in the table.
- `categorize`: `{"transactions": [{"date", "description", "amount", "category"}]}`.
- Empty: `{"months": []}` / `{"transactions": []}`.

## Error handling

Errors go to stderr as one line, prefix `csvledger: error: `, then exit with the code shown; stdout stays empty. `<path>` is exactly the argv string given on the command line (a relative path stays relative); `<line>` is `csv.reader.line_num` after reading the record. Row checks run in this order: field count, date, amount (transactions) or field count, category, type, pattern, priority, regex (rules). Header checks run in this order: (1) no header line, (2) duplicate column, (3) missing required column. For a duplicate column, `<name>` is the second occurrence after strip and lowercase, and the first duplicate in header order is reported. For a missing column, `<name>` is the first absent name in the listed order.

| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| File missing/unreadable | 3 / 4 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 / 4 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| No header line | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing header` |
| Duplicate header name (first duplicate in header order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: duplicate column '<name>'` |
| Required column absent (first in listed order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing column '<name>'` |
| Field count mismatch | 3 / 4 | `<path>:<line>: expected <N> fields, got <M>` |
| Bad date | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid date '<value>'` |
| Bad amount | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid amount '<value>'` |
| Empty category / pattern | 4 | `<path>:<line>: empty category` / `empty pattern` |
| Bad type | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid type '<value>'` |
| Bad priority | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid priority '<value>'` |
| Regex fails to compile | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid regex '<pattern>'` |
| argparse usage errors | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match the regex `^csvledger( report\| categorize)?: error: ` (argparse subparser prog form allowed) |

Warning (exit unaffected): `csvledger: warning: skipped <N> duplicate row(s)` when N > 0, written after stdout output. `<value>` is the stripped field value.

<result># csvledger codebase audit and spec input

## Key findings

**Repo state (verified with Glob and Read)**

1. The repo has one commit (`89ed938 seed: brief and contract`) and three tracked files: `brief.md`, `contract.md` and `.gitignore`.
   - There is no code, no `docs/`, no `tests/`, no `pyproject.toml`, no `pytest.ini`, no README, no `.gitattributes` and no `.editorconfig`. There are no conventions to inherit beyond `contract.md`.
   - `.gitignore` contains only `__pycache__/`.
   - The current branch is `master`, but the task says the main branch is `main`. `main` does not appear to exist locally, so PR targeting needs clarifying.
2. `brief.md` is one paragraph and adds nothing beyond `contract.md`. It confirms these requirements:
   - It must run as `python -m csvledger` from the repo root.
   - It uses the stdlib only.
   - Money must be exact.
   - Output must be byte-for-byte deterministic.
   - Errors must be clean and must never produce a traceback.
   - Pytest tests are required.
3. Everything must be created: `csvledger/` with `__init__.py` and `__main__.py`, the modules, `tests/`, and pytest config.

**Oracle checks**

I hand-verified the oracle cases against the rules.
- O1 Groceries: -45.10 + -12.005 = -57.105, which rounds to -57.11 under ROUND_HALF_UP, away from zero on ties.
- O5 Misc: income 0.125 gives 0.13, expenses -0.125 gives -0.13, and net 0 prints `0.00`.
- O5 Tiny: expenses of -0.004 quantize to -0.00 and must print `0.00`. Net is 0.006, which gives 0.01. Count is 3.
- O1 `Blue Bottle Cafe` matches both Coffee (priority 10) and Dining (priority 5). Priority must be compared as an int, and Coffee wins.
- O4's dedupe works because Decimal("-4.5") == Decimal("-4.50") and the descriptions are stripped. The dedupe key must therefore use the Decimal value, not the raw string.

**Gaps and risks found in the contract**

4. **Decimal context breaks exactness.** The default context has prec=28.
   - Sums of large or high-precision values are silently rounded.
   - `quantize` raises `InvalidOperation` when the result exceeds 28 digits.
   - The spec must require a high-precision local context, for example `decimal.Context(prec=MAX_PREC, Emax=MAX_EMAX)` with traps, or an equivalent exact approach. Otherwise very long amounts such as 40 digits give a wrong result or an exit-1 traceback.
5. **Huge priority literals.** `int()` on a string of more than 4300 digits raises `ValueError` in 3.11. A priority like `-?\d{5000}` would pass the regex and then crash with exit 1. The spec should either cap the length or define the behavior, for example comparing by sign and length, or catching the error as "invalid priority".
6. **`\d` matches Unicode digits.** With `re` on `str`, `\d` accepts Arabic-Indic and other digits, and `Decimal()` and `int()` accept them too.
   - The spec should say ASCII only (`re.ASCII` or `[0-9]`).
   - It should also say to use `fullmatch`, because `$` matches before a trailing `\n`. This matters for the `--month` regex, which is not stripped.
7. **Decoding is lazy.** If `csv.reader` iterates a text file object, `UnicodeDecodeError` can fire mid-file. A row error at line 2 would then win over invalid UTF-8 at line 100.
   - The contract implies "not valid UTF-8" is a file-level error.
   - Recommend reading the whole file as bytes, decoding with `utf-8-sig`, then passing `io.StringIO(text, newline="")` to `csv.reader`. This makes the order deterministic.
   - Mapping `OSError`, which includes a directory path and permission errors, to "cannot read file" is covered by the same step.
8. **`line_num` for multi-line quoted records.** `csv.reader.line_num` counts physical lines consumed, so after a multi-line record it is the record's last line, not its first. The contract says "after reading the record", so that is the defined behavior. The spec should state this explicitly and add a test.
   - A header that spans lines also advances `line_num`.
   - Lone `\r` also terminates a line in `csv.reader`.
9. **Header edge cases not specified.**
   - **Blank first line:** the reader yields `[]`. Is this "missing header", or is the blank skipped so the next row becomes the header? Recommend: "missing header" only when the reader yields no records at all. Otherwise the first record, even `[]`, is the header and fails the missing-column check. Pick one and test it.
   - **BOM-only file:** this decodes to empty text, so it is "missing header".
   - **Whitespace-only line:** it yields `['  ']`, one field, not zero fields. It is therefore not skipped and fails the field-count check.
   - **Header names:** they are stripped and lowercased, but cell values such as `type` are not lowercased. `Contains` is therefore an invalid type.
10. **`csv.Error` paths.** Fields over the 131072-character limit raise `csv.Error`. Unterminated quotes at EOF are accepted silently in non-strict mode. The spec should map `csv.Error` to a defined message and exit code, since none exists in the table. Suggestion: reuse `<path>:<line>: malformed CSV` with exit 3 or 4. Alternatively, call `csv.field_size_limit(sys.maxsize)` where it fits.
11. **Dedupe versus `--month`.** R5 is explicit: dedupe over all files first, then filter. Dedupe is also within a single file, and the warning N counts all duplicates, not just those in the requested month.
    - The key is `(date, stripped description, Decimal amount)`.
    - Description comparison is case-sensitive.
    - Dedupe is independent of category.

I also ran an argparse probe on the local Python 3.13.15 (Windows) to confirm behaviours the docs don't spell out. WebSearch was not needed because the official docs answered everything. ## Key findings

**argparse**
1. **Subparser prog.** `add_subparsers()` builds each subcommand's `prog` as `"<parent prog> <name>"`. With `ArgumentParser(prog="csvledger")`, `report` errors appear as `csvledger report: error: ...`. A missing or unknown subcommand gives `csvledger: error: ...`. This matches the contract regex `^csvledger( report| categorize)?: error: `. Python 3.14 changed how a custom parent `usage` affects subparser prog, so pass `prog=` explicitly if you set `usage=`.
2. **Error format and exit code.** `parser.error()` prints the usage block, then `<prog>: error: <msg>` to stderr, and exits 2. The last stderr line is therefore the `error:` line, which is what the contract asserts.
3. **Probe output on 3.13.** These are the messages you will see:
   - `csvledger report: error: the following arguments are required: FILE`
   - `csvledger report: error: argument --month: invalid month '2026-13' (expected YYYY-MM)`
   - `csvledger report: error: argument --format: invalid choice: 'xml' (choose from 'table', 'json')`
   - `csvledger: error: the following arguments are required: command`, with `add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)`
   - `csvledger: error: argument command: invalid choice: 'bogus' ...`
4. **Required subparser.** Use `required=True` together with `dest=`. Without `dest`, the missing-subcommand message is poorer.
5. **`nargs="+"` for FILE.** Use `add_argument("files", nargs="+", metavar="FILE")`. This gives the "required: FILE" error and the `FILE [FILE ...]` usage text.
6. **Dash handling.**

   - Do not use `argparse.FileType`. It maps `-` to stdin and is deprecated since 3.14.
   - Open paths yourself, so `-` is just a file name.
   - `--` ends option parsing, so `report -- -x` gives `files=['-x']`. `report -x` is a usage error (exit 2).
   - Options and positionals can interleave: `report a --month 2026-01` parses fine.
7. **`type=` validators.**
   - argparse catches `ArgumentTypeError`, `TypeError` and `ValueError` and formats them as `argument --month: <msg>`, exit 2.
   - The docs advise keeping `type=` validators simple, which a regex check is.
   - Use `choices=["table","json"]` for `--format`, with `default="table"`.
8. **Unicode digits in regexes.** Python `str` patterns make `\d` match any Unicode decimal digit, and `$` also matches before a trailing `\n`. The contract regexes use `\d` and `^...$`.

   - `Decimal()` and `int()` also accept non-ASCII digits, such as Arabic-Indic ones. Without ASCII-only matching, an `amount` like `"١٢"` would validate.
   - The contract wording is ambiguous here, so the spec must pin it down.
9. **`exit_on_error=False`.** It only covers `ArgumentError` and has gaps. Prefer the default behaviour, and map `SystemExit(2)` through unchanged.

**Streams and encoding**
10. **`reconfigure()` signature.** The signature is `reconfigure(*, encoding, errors, newline, line_buffering, write_through)`.
    - Passing `encoding` without `errors` resets `errors` to `'strict'`.
    - Encoding and newline can't change after data has been read from the stream, but changing them before any write is fine.
    - With `newline="\n"` (or `""`) on write, `\n` is not translated to `\r\n` on Windows. With `newline=None` it becomes `os.linesep`, so the contract needs the explicit value.
11. **Console and pipe defaults.**
    - On Windows, a console uses UTF-8, but pipes and files use the ANSI code page. My probe showed `cp1252`.
    - Stderr's handler is always `backslashreplace` and cannot be overridden through `PYTHONIOENCODING`.
    - `PYTHONUTF8=1` or `-X utf8` switches all streams to UTF-8.
12. **Stderr encoding on Windows.**
    - A non-ASCII path in an error message is written as `\xNN` or `\uNNNN` escapes when stderr is a pipe under cp1252. The raw UTF-8 bytes will not appear.
    - To guarantee UTF-8 on stderr, also call `sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="backslashreplace", newline="\n")`. The contract only mandates reconfiguring stdout.
    - Tests that check non-ASCII stderr text need to decode with the right encoding or set `PYTHONUTF8=1` / `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`.
13. **Streams can be `None` or lack `.buffer`.** The docs say `sys.stdout` may be `None` (pythonw) or replaced by `StringIO`, which has no `.buffer`. Guard with `hasattr(stream, "reconfigure")`.
14. **Stdout stays empty on error.** To keep it empty on every error path (R2, R3), build the full output string in memory and write it once at the end. Write the duplicate warning to stderr after stdout.
15. **Flush failures.** If flushing stdout fails at interpreter shutdown (for example a broken pipe), the exit code becomes 120. Flush explicitly inside the handler and decide what a `BrokenPipeError` should map to.

**Entry point and exit codes**
16. **`__main__.py` convention.** The docs prefer a minimal `__main__.py` with no `__name__` guard. Put the logic in `csvledger/cli.py` with `def main(argv=None) -> int`, and have `__main__.py` do `from .cli import main; import sys; sys.exit(main())`. That keeps `main` importable and unit-testable.
17. **Exit-code semantics.**
    - `sys.exit(int)` is the exit status. `sys.exit("str")` prints the string and exits 1, so never use it.
    - An uncaught exception also exits 1, with a traceback.
    - The contract reserves 1 for unexpected internal errors "never intentional", so a catch-all handler must still return 1 but with a clean one-line message.
    - Expected failures use dedicated exception classes (`TransactionFileError` → 3, `RulesFileError` → 4) and are caught in `main()`.
    - The catch-all `except Exception` prints `csvledger: error: internal error: <ExcType>` (no traceback) and returns 1.
    - `SystemExit` from argparse passes through (do not catch it with `except Exception`; it derives from `BaseException`).

    - `RecursionError` and `MemoryError` are `Exception` subclasses, so the catch-all handles them.

18. **Subprocess pattern.** The pytest pattern is `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "csvledger", ...], cwd=REPO_ROOT, capture_output=True, env=env)`.

<result># Research report: stdlib-only csvledger (Python 3.11+)

I read `contract.md` and `brief.md` (the repo has only those two files, no code). I fetched the official docs for `csv`, `decimal`, `re` and `stdtypes`. I also ran probes on Python 3.13.15, marked "(probe)" below. I did not run them on 3.11 and 3.12. No files were created or modified.

## Key findings

1. **`newline=""`.** The csv docs say a file object "should be opened with `newline=''`". Without it, newlines inside quoted fields are mis-read. The contract already requires it. The module does its own universal newline handling, and a bare `\r` also ends a record (probe: `'1,2\r3,4'` gives two rows).

2. **`line_num` counts source lines, not records.** The docs say it is "the number of lines read from the source iterator... not the same as the number of records". After a multiline record it points at the record's last line. Probes:
   - `a,b\n\n"x\ny",2\n` gives line_num 1, 2 (the blank row), then 4 for the multiline record, which starts on line 3.
   - Blank lines count toward `line_num`.
   - The contract's "`<line>` is `csv.reader.line_num` after reading the record" is therefore the last physical line of a multiline record.

3. **Blank lines and whitespace-only lines differ.**
   - A truly empty line yields `[]` (probe). The contract skips these.
   - A line of only spaces, `"  "`, yields `['  ']`, a one-field row. It is not skipped and hits the field-count error.
   - `,` yields `['', '']`.
   - Do not test `if not any(row)` or `row == ['']`. Test `len(row) == 0`.
   - The docs page does not mention empty rows. Only the probe confirms it.

4. **Non-strict reader is lenient, and the contract mandates it.** The docs say `strict` defaults to False and, when True, raises `Error` on bad input.
   - In the default mode, `a,"b\n` (unterminated quote) returns `['a','b\n']` with no error (probe).
   - `a,"b"c,d` returns `['a','bc','d']`.
   - So the only `csv.Error` reachable under the contract is the field-size limit. The default is 131072 and the probe raised `field larger than field limit (131072)`.
   - The contract has no row for `csv.Error`. A malformed quote can silently swallow the rest of the file into one field, which then surfaces as a field-count error.

5. **BOM handling.**
   - `utf-8-sig` strips only one leading BOM. A second U+FEFF stays in the first header name (probe).
   - `str.strip()` does not remove U+FEFF, so the first column becomes `\ufeffdate` and the run fails with "missing column 'date'". This is acceptable but should be stated.
   - The docs page does not cover BOM.

6. **UTF-8 errors surface lazily.**
   - A `UnicodeDecodeError` is raised during iteration, not at `open()`.
   - If the spec means "not valid UTF-8" to take precedence, the file must be read and decoded before the row checks run. Otherwise a bad row earlier in the file wins.
   - `OSError` covers a missing file, a directory (`IsADirectoryError`) and permission errors.
   - Also catch `csv.Error`.

7. **Decimal rounding.**
   - `quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_HALF_UP)` rounds ties away from zero: 0.125 gives 0.13, -0.125 gives -0.13, -0.005 gives -0.01, and 0.005 gives 0.01 (probe, matching O5).
   - The default context rounding is ROUND_HALF_EVEN, so the rounding mode must be passed explicitly or `quantize` is wrong.

8. **Negative zero is real.**
   - `Decimal('-0.004').quantize(...)` gives `Decimal('-0.00')`, and `format(q,'f')` prints `-0.00` (probe).
   - `Decimal('-0')` and `Decimal('-0.00')` also print `-0.00`.
   - The contract's `if q == 0: "0.00"` rule is therefore necessary. `-0.00 == 0` is True.
   - It must be applied to every displayed money value: per-transaction amounts, income, expenses, net, and the JSON strings.

9. **Context precision threatens "exact".** The default precision is 28 (docs).
   - Addition in `sum()` is rounded to 28 significant digits.
   - Probe: `Decimal('1'*40) + Decimal('1')` gives `1.111...E+39`, which is inexact and in exponent notation.
   - The docs say `quantize` signals `InvalidOperation` if the quantized coefficient would exceed precision. Probe: `Decimal('9'*30).quantize(...)` raises `InvalidOperation`.
   - The contract's amount regex `^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$` has no length bound.
   - A 27 or more digit amount therefore causes either a traceback or a silently inexact sum. A 28-digit sum of several amounts can also overflow.
   - Fix: run arithmetic and quantize inside a high-precision context, for example `decimal.Context(prec=...)` or `localcontext(prec=...)`. `localcontext` keyword arguments are supported since 3.11. Alternatively, define a maximum length.

10. **The Decimal constructor is permissive.**
    - It accepts surrounding whitespace, underscores, exponents, `NaN`, `Infinity`, and non-ASCII Nd digits.
    - Probe: `Decimal("١٢٣.٥")` gives `12.5`.
    - Validate with the regex first, then construct. Never rely on `Decimal()` raising to reject input.

11. **Regex pitfalls (docs plus probes).**
    - `\d` in a str pattern matches any Unicode Nd digit unless `re.ASCII` is used. `^\d+$` matches Arabic-Indic digits, and `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` matches a string starting with fullwidth `２` (probe).
    - `$` matches at the end or just before a trailing newline. `^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$` accepts `"12\n"` (probe). A quoted multiline field can end in a newline, but `strip()` removes it first. Still, `$` is unsafe as written for `--month`.
    - `fullmatch` with `[0-9]` or `re.ASCII` avoids both problems (probe: both `fullmatch` forms reject `"12\n"`).
    - `\Z` is documented as identical to `\z`, so it also works.
    - A fullwidth-digit date string passes the regex but `date.fromisoformat` rejects it. Python 3.11+ `fromisoformat` also accepts `20260101` and `2026-W01-1`. This is why the contract says "regex first".
    - Year `0000` passes the regex and must be rejected by `date()` as an invalid date, which is covered by "valid calendar date".
    - Rules `priority` `^-?\d+$` has the same Unicode-digit issue. `int()` accepts Unicode digits too. `int()` also raises `ValueError` for strings over 4300 digits (the int-str conversion limit), which would give a traceback unless caught as "invalid priority".

12. **`strip()` versus Unicode whitespace.**
    - No-argument `strip()` uses `str.isspace()`. It removes NBSP U+00A0, U+2003, `\x1c`-`\x1f` and U+0085.
    - It does not remove U+200B or U+FEFF (probe).
    - The spec should say "`str.strip()` with no arguments" explicitly, so `\xa0` and similar are stripped from descriptions, headers and amounts. A dedup key built from stripped descriptions depends on this.
    - Note the splitlines boundary list (`\x1c`, `\x85`, `\u2028` and others). `csv` does not split on these, so they can sit inside fields.

13. **`casefold`.**
    - `casefold()` is more aggressive than `lower()`: `ß` becomes `ss`.
    - `contains` uses casefold on both sides, so a pattern `ß` matches `SS`, and a pattern `strasse` matches `Straße`.
    - `regex` uses `re.IGNORECASE` instead (probe: `re.search('straße','STRASSE',re.I)` is None). The two rule types therefore differ in Unicode matching. This is deliberate in the contract but a trap for tests.
    - Header names use `lower()` per the contract wording ("lowercased"). `casefold` and `lower` differ for a few characters, such as `ß` and `İ`. State which one applies.

14. **`re.search` can raise more than `re.error`.** `re.compile` can raise `re.error`, and rarely `RecursionError` or `OverflowError`, for pathological patterns. Catch broadly at load time so the exit code is 4. Catastrophic backtracking at match time cannot be prevented with the stdlib alone.

15. **Embedded newlines and `\r` in descriptions.**
    - A quoted description can contain `\r\n`, `\n` or `\r`.
    - In the `categorize` table these are written raw, which breaks alignment and violates AC10 ("no `\r`").
    - JSON escapes them.
    - The contract does not say how tables render such characters.

16. **Width and rstrip.**
    - `len()` on code points means East Asian wide characters and combining marks misalign. This is contractually fine, since the contract says to use `len()`.
    - "Each line right-stripped": `rstrip()` with no args also strips Unicode whitespace and `\x85`. Use `rstrip(" ")` if only spaces are meant.

17. **Sorting.** Default `str` sorting is by code point (locale-independent). Sorting by key `(month, category)` is stable and deterministic. Dates in `categorize` are validated ASCII `YYYY-MM-DD`, so string order equals date order. Python's `sorted` is stable, which gives the "ties in input order" rule.

18. **stdout and stderr.**
    - `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` prevents `\r\n` translation on Windows.
    - stderr is not reconfigured by the contract. On Windows (cp1252 or similar), a path or value containing non-encodable characters can raise `UnicodeEncodeError` while writing the error message, which gives a traceback. Reconfigure stderr to UTF-8 with `errors="backslashreplace"`.
    - The warning must come after stdout is flushed.

19. **Hash and equality for dedup.** `Decimal('-4.5') == Decimal('-4.50')` and they hash equal, as do `Decimal('-0')` and `Decimal('0')`. The key `(date, stripped_desc, Decimal)` matches the contract's "numeric amount value" (O4). Dedup is case-sensitive and does not casefold.

20. **Python 3.13 note.** `\z` was added in 3.14, so avoid it and use `fullmatch`. This keeps 3.11 compatibility.

## Constraints the spec MUST respect

- The CSV reader must use `csv.reader` defaults (non-strict) on a file opened with `newline=""` and `encoding="utf-8-sig"`. `<line>` is `reader.line_num`.
- Blank-row skipping applies only to `len(row) == 0`. Whitespace-only lines are field-count errors.
- Every validation regex must be ASCII-only and anchored with `fullmatch` (or `re.ASCII` plus `\Z`/`fullmatch`). This covers date, amount, priority and `--month`. The contract's `^...$` notation is shorthand, and a literal `$` would accept a trailing `\n`. The `--month` regex literal in the contract has the same issue.
- Money display must special-case `q == 0` and quantize with an explicit ROUND_HALF_UP. Rounding happens once, at display, never on stored values or sums.
- Sums must be exact despite the 28-digit default precision. Either use a context with enough precision, or reject over-long numbers.
- All decoding, OS, csv and Decimal failures must map to exit 3 or 4, never a traceback.
- A broad top-level handler maps unexpected exceptions to exit 1. stdout must be empty on exit 3 and 4, so build the output string fully before writing.
- Load order is rules first, then transaction files. The first error wins.
- Row checks follow the contract's order. Header checks are no header, then duplicate, then missing.

## Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD add)

1. **Sanity-check the "exact" claim for large values.** Specify a Decimal context, for example `Context(prec=100, rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)` plus a cap on digits per amount. Also state what exit code and message apply beyond the cap, or state that no cap exists and precision is unlimited by using `MAX_PREC`.
2. **Pin down edge behaviors the contract is silent on:**
   - A file that starts with a blank line, or is only a BOM or only `\n`. State whether the first record is the header even if empty (`[]`), or whether it counts as "missing header".
   - A `csv.Error` such as the field size limit. State the message and exit code (for example `<path>:<line>: malformed CSV`, exit 3 or 4).
   - UTF-8 errors versus earlier row errors. State precedence by reading and decoding the whole file first.
   - A second leading BOM.
3. **Table rendering of control characters.** Either replace `\r`, `\n` and similar in cells with a visible escape, or accept raw output and drop AC10 for table output. Also decide on `rstrip` versus `rstrip(" ")`.
4. **Guard `int(priority)`.** Catch `ValueError` for strings over 4300 digits, or cap the length.
5. **Header lowercasing.** Say `str.lower()` versus `casefold()`, and say that `strip()` takes no arguments.
6. **Error output.** Force stderr to UTF-8 with `errors="backslashreplace"`. Mention argparse's `allow_abbrev` (default True), so `--form json` is accepted unless disabled. `-` as an ordinary file name works with argparse as a positional.
7. **Tests the spec should require:**
   - Fullwidth and Arabic digits in date, amount, `--month` and priority.
   - `"12\n"` as a quoted amount.
   - A multiline quoted description before a bad row, to verify `line_num`.
   - Whitespace-only rows.
   - `-0.004`, `-0`, `-0.00` and `0.005`-style ties.
   - A 30-digit amount.
   - NBSP-padded description dedup.
   - Cross-platform identical bytes. Run on Windows and compare, with no `\r` in output.
8. **Add `__main__.py`.** Use `sys.exit(main())`.

1. **`newline=""`.** The csv docs say a file object "should be opened with `newline=''`". Without it, newlines inside quoted fields are mis-read. The contract already requires it. 3. **Blank lines and whitespace-only lines differ.**
